history_of_present_illness: Rat bite fever is characterized by a relapsing type of fever following a rat bite, typically after an incubation period of six to eight weeks, during which the wound heals. Onset is sudden with rigors, headache, nausea, and marked weakness. The cicatrix becomes inflamed, with surrounding tissues showing oedema and sometimes vesicle formation. Tender lymphatics extend from the inflamed area to swollen lymphatic glands. The fever rises rapidly to 101-102°F, reaching about 104°F within two to three days, remaining high for several days before rapidly falling to normal with profuse sweating. This is followed by an apyrexial period, during which local inflammation subsides, before the fever relapses. Numerous relapses can occur over weeks, months, or even years, with successive paroxysms usually being less severe. An eruption of purplish spots may appear on the chest and arms, along with urticarial lesions, joint pains, and motor/sensory disturbances. Symptoms of nephritis may also appear. The course of the disease can extend over several months, with up to twelve febrile accessions.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The disease is caused by the spirochaete *Leptospira morsus-muris*. In a study by Futaki and others (1915), spirochaetes about 10 microns long were found in bite area tissues and adjacent lymphatic glands. Shorter, thicker spirochaetes (3-6 microns) are found in the blood of humans and infected animals, while longer forms (up to 20 microns) are seen in culture. *Leptospira morsus-muris* is present in the blood of infected mice, rats, or guinea pigs during the first two weeks post-infection, then disseminates into connective tissues, particularly of the lips, bridge of the nose, and tongue. Transmission to humans occurs through a bite wound, where spirochaete-containing tissues are inoculated, not typically via saliva. The organism may also be excreted in urine. Epidemiologically, about 3% of house-rats in Japan are carriers. The disease is less frequent in other countries but has been reported in various European countries, America, China, and Australia. The construction of Japanese houses is believed to provide greater opportunities for rat bites.
vitals: During the pyrexial period, the fever rises rapidly to 101-102°F and can reach about 104°F, remaining high for two to three days. The pulse is rapid and weak.
physical_exam: Inflammatory signs develop in the cicatrix, accompanied by lymphangitis and swelling of tributary lymphatic glands. The cicatrix can become inflamed with surrounding oedema and vesicle formation. Lines of tender lymphatics extend to swollen lymphatic glands. There may be an eruption of purplish spots, chiefly on the chest and arms, and urticarial lesions. Joint pains, motor, and sensory disturbances can be noted. Prostration is present during febrile periods. In infected guinea pigs, swelling of lymphatic glands and spleen is observed.
labs_and_diagnostics: Spirochaetes (*Leptospira morsus-muris*) are found in the tissues of the bite area and adjacent lymphatic glands (about 10 microns long). In the blood of humans and infected animals, shorter, thicker spirochaetes (3-6 microns) are observed. Cultivated forms can reach up to 20 microns. During the febrile paroxysm, there is eosinophilia and leucocytosis of about 15,000. Spirochaetes should be sought in the blood during early febrile periods, with dark-field illumination being the best method for their demonstration. Pathological findings in infected guinea pigs include swelling of lymphatic glands and spleen with spirochaetes. The liver is congested and may contain spirochaetes. Human autopsies reveal degenerative changes in the liver and kidneys.
differential_diagnosis: The fever pattern is suggestive of relapsing fevers.
management_and_clinical_course: Treatment is entirely symptomatic. Salvarsan has shown some success. Strychnine is recommended for heart weakness, and tonics are advised during convalescence. Aspirin is often necessary to relieve headache and joint pains. As prophylactic measures, wound cauterization, similar to that observed in rabies, should be considered. The infection is rarely fatal in experimental animals, but causes about a 10% mortality in humans.
